people.name: Pancho Segura
body: On a tennis court in the 1940s, a small young man from Guayaquil, Ecuador, gripped his racket with both hands to hit a forehand. Coaches of the day thought that was a mistake. Francisco "Pancho" Segura made it his main weapon, and Jack Kramer, one of the sport's greats, called it the best shot in tennis history, according to the International Tennis Hall of Fame.

Segura was born on June 20, 1921, in Guayaquil, Ecuador's big port city. The Hall of Fame says his family was very poor and that his father earned about $300 a year. He came to the United States and enrolled at the University of Miami, where he won three NCAA singles titles in a row, from 1943 to 1945.

At that time the best players often turned professional and toured together, city to city. Segura joined the pro tour led by Kramer in 1948 and was at one point co-ranked number one in the world. He won the U.S. Pro Championships singles title every year from 1950 to 1952.

His second career may have mattered even more. Segura became one of the best-known coaches in American tennis. He began working daily with Jimmy Connors just as Connors turned 16, helping shape a future world number one. The Hall of Fame's memorial to him called him "the best mind" in its headline, and Stan Smith called him one of the most brilliant tactical minds he had met in the sport.
Segura died on November 18, 2017, at age 96, at his home in Carlsbad, California, of complications from Parkinson's disease, according to his son.
keyFacts: 1921: Born June 20 in Guayaquil, Ecuador.
1943–1945: Won three straight NCAA singles titles for the University of Miami.
1948: Joined the professional tour led by Jack Kramer.
1950–1952: Won the U.S. Pro Championships singles title three years running.
1970: Inducted into the University of Miami Sports Hall of Fame.
1984: Inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame.
2017: Died November 18 in Carlsbad, California, at age 96.

people.name: Francisco Moya
body: Francisco Moya grew up in Corona, Queens, playing soccer as a kid in Flushing Meadows Corona Park. Years later, as an elected official, he pushed for a professional soccer stadium in the same part of Queens.

Moya was born at Elmhurst Hospital and raised in Corona. In 2010 he won the Democratic primary for New York's 39th Assembly District, covering parts of Corona, Jackson Heights and Elmhurst, with more than 66 percent of the vote, then won the seat. QNS reported at the time that he would be the first Ecuadorian American elected to state office in New York. In the Assembly he wrote legislation to give undocumented students access to state financial aid and scholarships.

In 2018 he moved to the New York City Council, serving a Queens district until the end of 2025. He helped strengthen the city's sanctuary protections and championed the Willets Point development, which pairs a soccer stadium for New York City Football Club with about 2,500 affordable housing units, a school and community space. In 2025 he highlighted the first celebration of Ecuadorian Heritage Month at Gracie Mansion, the mayor's residence.
When he left the Council he told City & State that he was not ruling out a return to public office.
keyFacts: Born at Elmhurst Hospital; raised in Corona, Queens.
2010: Won New York State Assembly District 39.
In the Assembly: wrote legislation giving undocumented students access to state financial aid.
2018–2025: New York City Council, District 21 (Queens).
Championed the Willets Point soccer stadium and affordable housing project.

people.name: Jose Garces
body: Jose Garces says his cooking began with his paternal grandmother, Mamita Amada, who introduced him to Latin cooking when he was young. He was raised in Chicago by parents from Ecuador.

Garces trained at Kendall College's School of Culinary Arts in Chicago, then worked in kitchens in Spain and New York City. In 2001 he moved to Philadelphia, and in 2005 he opened his first restaurant, Amada, a Spanish tapas restaurant. As of October 2026, the Garces Group's website lists Amada, in Philadelphia, Radnor and Atlantic City, along with Okatshe, Rural Society and Village Whiskey. The group's undated biography of him also describes an events and catering business and a 40-acre organic farm in Bucks County, Pennsylvania.
In 2009 the James Beard Foundation named him Best Chef, Mid-Atlantic. He also won Food Network's "The Next Iron Chef," beating nine other chefs. He founded a nonprofit, the Garces Foundation.

people.name: Nina Vaca
body: Nina Vaca started her company in her living room in Dallas, Texas, in 1996, when she was 25. That small start became Pinnacle Group, a workforce and information-technology services company. NBC News described it in 2015 as the fastest-growing woman-owned business in America, and the company calls itself the largest Hispanic-owned workforce solutions company in North America.

Vaca was born in Quito, Ecuador's capital. Her family had run a general store there selling everything from tractors to dynamite for construction. Her mother's wish to travel led the family to emigrate, and they settled in Los Angeles. She told NBC News that giving up everything in Ecuador involved "a lot of faith, humility and gratitude." Al Día reports that her parents ran a travel agency in Los Angeles and that the company nearly went under after September 11, 2001.

As the company grew, so did her public role. She chaired the U.S. Hispanic Chamber of Commerce, the first Ecuadorian to do so, and in 2014 was named one of the first Presidential Ambassadors for Global Entrepreneurship. By 2015 she sat on the boards of Kohl's and Comerica Bank and was the first woman director of Cinemark Holdings. As of October 2026, Pinnacle's site lists her as Chairman and CEO.
keyFacts: Born in Quito, Ecuador; family settled in Los Angeles.
1996: Founded Pinnacle Group in her Dallas living room.
2014: Named one of the inaugural Presidential Ambassadors for Global Entrepreneurship.
First Ecuadorian to chair the U.S. Hispanic Chamber of Commerce; later Chairman Emeritus.
As of October 2026: Chairman and CEO of Pinnacle Group.

people.name: Cecilia Alvear
body: In 1982 NBC News needed someone to run its Mexico City bureau. It chose Cecilia Alvear, and NBC reports she was the first Latina to hold that job. She would spend much of her life opening newsroom doors for other Latinos.

Alvear was a native of Ecuador. In Los Angeles she worked for several local NBC stations until 1982, when the network sent her to Mexico City. Over about 25 years with NBC she worked as a producer covering Latin America and the West Coast.
NBC News reports that she was the first Latina chosen for a Nieman Fellowship at Harvard, in 1988. The Nieman Foundation lists her in its class of 1989.

Alvear was a founding member of the National Association of Hispanic Journalists and later its president, and the association inducted her into its Hall of Fame in 2007. A fellow Nieman recalled the advice Alvear wrote to her: "You have to give back. Someone helped you, now you help someone." She died of breast cancer on April 21, 2017, in Santa Monica, California, at age 77.

1982: Became NBC News Mexico City bureau chief.

people.name: David Fraser-Hidalgo
body: Before he wrote laws, David Fraser-Hidalgo enforced them. From 1994 to 1997 he was a police officer in Montgomery County, Maryland, the suburban county where he grew up after being born in Quito, Ecuador.

Fraser-Hidalgo went to Albert Einstein High School in Kensington, Maryland, and earned a history degree from St. Mary's College of Maryland in 1992. After his police service he worked in business, in website marketing and sales for Sandglass Systems and then as a sales manager and director for Regus. He also served on the board of the Hispanic Chamber of Commerce of Montgomery County and the advisory board of the Montgomery County Chamber of Commerce.

In October 2013 he was appointed to the Maryland House of Delegates for District 15, and he won election in 2014. He chaired the Motor Vehicles and Transportation Subcommittee from 2019 to 2023 and the Property and Casualty Insurance Subcommittee from 2023 to 2025. The General Assembly's site, last updated in June 2026, lists him as a delegate and as chair of the Energy Subcommittee. Maryland's House seats are on the ballot on November 3, 2026.

He joined the Maryland Legislative Latino Caucus early in his service (the General Assembly's site says 2015, the Maryland Manual 2014) and chaired it from 2019 to 2024. Mothers Against Drunk Driving named him Legislator of the Year in 2016.

1992: B.A. in history, St. Mary's College of Maryland.

2013: Appointed to the Maryland House of Delegates, District 15; elected 2014.
2019–2024: Chair, Maryland Legislative Latino Caucus.
2016: Mothers Against Drunk Driving Legislator of the Year.

people.name: Jaime Jarrín
body: Jaime Jarrín came to Los Angeles from a country where soccer, not baseball, was the sport he had grown up with. For 64 years his voice carried Dodgers baseball in Spanish to listeners across Southern California.

Jarrín was born on December 10, 1935, in Ecuador. The Baseball Hall of Fame gives his birthplace as Cayambe, while The World and the Walter O'Malley Dodger history site say Quito. He earned degrees in philosophy, literature and journalism in Quito. The Hall of Fame and The World say he came to the United States in 1955. In East Los Angeles he worked in a factory making fences while he looked for news work at KWKW, a Spanish-language radio station, where he first got a few weekend hours.

The Dodgers moved from Brooklyn to Los Angeles in 1958, and KWKW began carrying their games in Spanish. Jarrín called his first Dodgers game on April 14, 1959, and became the team's Spanish-language play-by-play voice, learning a sport he had not grown up with. In 1970 he became the first Latin American to win the Golden Mike award. His home-run call, "¡Se va, se va, se va, y despídala con un beso!", became famous. Pitching star Fernando Valenzuela later worked beside him in the booth for more than a decade. Over his career he called 25 All-Star Games and 25 World Series.

In 1998 the National Baseball Hall of Fame honored him with the Ford C. Frick Award for broadcasting. Jarrín retired after the 2022 season, and the Dodgers held a ceremony for him on October 1, 2022, attended by Valenzuela, Mayor Eric Garcetti, Senator Alex Padilla and actor Edward James Olmos.
keyFacts: December 10, 1935: Born in Ecuador.
1955: Came to the United States, by the Hall of Fame's account.
April 14, 1959: Called his first Dodgers game on KWKW.
1970: First Latin American to win the Golden Mike award.
1998: Received the Baseball Hall of Fame's Ford C. Frick Award.
Called 25 All-Star Games and 25 World Series.
2022: Retired after 64 seasons.

people.name: Lourdes G. Baird
body: In 1971, at 36 or so, Lourdes Baird finished an associate's degree at Los Angeles City College. Within about twenty years she would be the chief federal prosecutor for one of the largest federal districts in the country, and then a federal judge.
Baird was born in 1935 in Quito, Ecuador. After Los Angeles City College she earned a bachelor's degree from UCLA in 1973 and a law degree from UCLA School of Law in 1976.

She joined the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of California as an assistant U.S. attorney from 1977 to 1983. After three years in private practice, she became a judge in 1986, serving on the East Los Angeles Municipal Court, the Los Angeles Municipal Court and then the Los Angeles County Superior Court until 1990.

In 1990 she returned to the U.S. Attorney's Office as the U.S. Attorney, leading it until 1992. On April 2, 1992, President George H. W. Bush nominated her to the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, and the Senate confirmed her on August 11, 1992. She took senior status in 2004 and retired from the bench in 2005. After that she worked as an arbitrator and mediator. The Los Angeles County Bar Association named her Outstanding Jurist of the Year in 2001, and the Daily Journal later listed her among California's top neutrals. Los Angeles County's biography of her notes that she is fluent in Spanish.
keyFacts: 1935: Born in Quito, Ecuador.
1971: Associate's degree, Los Angeles City College.
1976: J.D., UCLA School of Law.
1977–1983: Assistant U.S. Attorney, Central District of California.
1986–1990: Municipal and Superior Court judge in Los Angeles.
1990–1992: U.S. Attorney, Central District of California.
1992–2005: U.S. District Judge (senior status 2004; retired 2005).
2001: Los Angeles County Bar Association Outstanding Jurist of the Year.

people.name: Carmen R. Velasquez
body: Carmen Velasquez left Ecuador at 14 without speaking a word of English. Advisers told her to become a secretary instead of a lawyer. She attended Long Island City High School, worked as a fruit-store cashier, factory worker, secretary and bank teller, and built her life and career in Queens, New York. Voters there elected her a judge. The Carnegie Corporation of New York calls her the first Ecuadorian American judge in the United States, though Lourdes Baird, born in Quito, was a Los Angeles judge from 1986.

She studied at John Jay College of Criminal Justice and earned her law degree at Temple Law School on a CLEO fellowship and a Temple graduate fellowship. She was an assistant district attorney in the Bronx, then a deputy advocate in the legal affairs division of the New York City Sanitation Department, before opening a private practice in 1991 in criminal defense, family and immigration law.

As a lawyer, Velasquez did a great deal of pro bono work for people who could not afford a lawyer. "It has not been easy for me," she has said, "but I am grateful for the opportunity to attend school and get an education." She was a founding member and past president of the Latino Lawyers Association of Queens County.

In New York, many judges are elected. Velasquez was elected to the New York City Civil Court on November 4, 2008, then in 2014 won a seat on the New York State Supreme Court, 11th Judicial District, which covers Queens. In New York, the Supreme Court is the main trial-level court. In January 2021 she was sworn in as president of the Association of Justices of the Supreme Court of the State of New York, the first Latina to lead the group, according to the Queens Daily Eagle. As of October 2026, amNY describes her as a Queens Supreme Court justice, and reports that the Latino Lawyers Association named its main annual award after her.

John Jay College of Criminal Justice; J.D., Temple Law School.

people.name: Debbie Mucarsel-Powell
body: As a teenager newly arrived in California, Debbie Mucarsel-Powell worked the morning shift at a doughnut shop before school, helping to support her family. Years later she became the first Ecuadorian American and the first South American-born immigrant to serve in the U.S. Congress, according to the Carnegie Corporation of New York.

She was born in Ecuador and moved to the United States at 14 with her mother and sisters. She earned a bachelor's degree in political science from Pitzer College and a master's degree in international political economy from Claremont Graduate University. In 1996 she moved to Florida, where she raised money for nonprofits including the Hope Center, the Zoo Miami Foundation and the Coral Restoration Foundation. At Florida International University she held several posts, including associate dean in the College of Medicine.

When she was 24, her father was killed outside his home in Ecuador. In Congress she joined the Gun Violence Prevention Task Force and pushed for universal background checks and a ban on assault rifles, according to her official House biography.

In 2018 she won election to represent Florida's 26th Congressional District, which stretches from the Miami area to the Florida Keys. She served on the House Judiciary Committee during her one term, 2019 to 2021. In 2024 she won the Democratic nomination for the U.S. Senate in Florida and lost to Senator Rick Scott. She has been a senior advisor to the gun-safety group Giffords. As of October 2026, George Washington University's site lists her as executive director of its Graduate School of Political Management.

B.A., Pitzer College; M.A., Claremont Graduate University.

people.name: Evelyn Sanguinetti
body: On the day she was sworn in as lieutenant governor of Illinois in January 2015, Evelyn Sanguinetti learned something she had not known: she was announced as the first Latina lieutenant governor in the country. She told NPR Illinois that she did not like the word "trailblazer." She called herself a "peligrosa," a dangerous woman.

Sanguinetti was born to teenage parents in Hialeah, Florida, and grew up with Spanish as her first language. Her mother came to the United States as a Cuban refugee and her father immigrated from Ecuador. She earned a bachelor's degree in piano performance from Florida International University and a law degree from John Marshall Law School in Chicago.
She worked as an assistant Illinois attorney general under Attorney General Jim Ryan, and her first elected office was local: she served on the city council of Wheaton, a western Chicago suburb.

In 2014 Republican Bruce Rauner chose her as his running mate, and they won that November. She served until January 2019, and Southern Illinois University described her as the first Hispanic and Latina to hold statewide office in Illinois. She chaired a bipartisan task force on consolidating local government and cutting unfunded mandates, which made 27 recommendations. She also co-chaired the state's Opioid Overdose Prevention Task Force, whose work led to a telephone helpline and a standing order that made the overdose-reversal drug Narcan available at pharmacies. She said she visited all 102 Illinois counties.

people.name: F. Javier Cevallos
body: F. Javier Cevallos spent most of his childhood in the highlands around Cuenca, Ecuador. When he was 14, his family moved to Puerto Rico. Decades later he would lead two American public universities.

Cuenca is the capital of Azuay province, in the southern Andes. Cevallos's own route north passed through Puerto Rico, where he finished his bachelor's degree at the University of Puerto Rico at Mayagüez. He then followed his brother to the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and earned a master's degree and a Ph.D.

He became a scholar of Latin American literature. In 1981 he began teaching Spanish as an assistant professor at the University of Maine at Orono. He then moved to the University of Massachusetts Amherst, where he became a full professor and chaired the Department of Spanish and Portuguese. He moved into university administration in 1994.

In 2002 he became president of Kutztown University in Pennsylvania and served there for 12 years. In July 2014 he became the 16th president of Framingham State University in Massachusetts. He led it for nearly eight years and retired in 2022 after about four decades in academia. He then took a one-year post as President-in-Residence at Harvard's Graduate School of Education for 2022–23.

people.name: Charles Castronovo
body: As a boy, Charles Castronovo acted in school plays and played in three rock bands. Few people in his family were musicians, but, as he told the blog Opera Traveller, the family was "very colourful and loud and open." He went on to become an opera tenor who has sung at the Metropolitan Opera, the Royal Opera House in London, and the Vienna and Berlin State Operas.

Castronovo was born in 1975 in Queens, New York. Both of his parents were immigrants. His mother came from Ecuador at about 15, and his father came from Sicily at about 16. He has said that his father spoke Sicilian and his mother spoke Spanish, and that the languages were always mixed at home. He credits that with giving him a good ear for languages.

He studied music at Cal State Fullerton, where he sang in musicals such as Oklahoma!, Brigadoon and West Side Story, began his career in the chorus of the Los Angeles Opera, and then joined the Metropolitan Opera's Lindemann Young Artist Development Program in New York. He made his Met debut in 1999 as Beppe in Pagliacci.

From there he built an international career, including Tamino in The Magic Flute, Ferrando in Così fan tutte, Alfredo in La traviata and Rodolfo in La bohème. At Los Angeles Opera he starred as Mario, the postman, in Daniel Catán's Il Postino opposite Plácido Domingo. In 2014 he told Opera Traveller that his next idea was a small-group project of Spanish and Latin American music from his mother's side of the family.

Began in the Los Angeles Opera chorus; went through the Met's Lindemann Young Artist program.

people.name: Irina Falconi
body: In April 2016 a magnitude-7.8 earthquake struck Portoviejo, Ecuador. Tennis.com reported that it killed more than 400 people and leveled the house where tennis player Irina Falconi had been born. The next day, playing in Bogotá, Colombia, Falconi won her first title on the WTA, the main women's professional tour. She called the win bittersweet and said she would donate to victims and their families.

Falconi was born on May 4, 1990, in Portoviejo, a city in the coastal province of Manabí. She grew up in New York City and finished high school in Florida. Her father, Carlos, had been a professional soccer player. She represented the United States as a player.

She played college tennis at Georgia Tech, where she was an All-American in singles in 2009 and 2010 and the 2010 Atlantic Coast Conference Player of the Year. At the 2011 Pan American Games in Guadalajara, Mexico, she won the gold medal in women's singles and silver in doubles with Christina McHale.

Her Bogotá title came at the 2016 Copa Colsanitas, where, seeded fifth, she beat Spain's Sílvia Soler Espinosa 6–2, 2–6, 6–4. Her father was in Portoviejo during the earthquake and stayed in Ecuador afterward to help with the recovery. A month later, on May 23, 2016, she reached her career-high singles ranking of No. 63, according to the WTA, which now lists her as retired, under the name Irina Falconi Hartman.
keyFacts: 1990: Born May 4 in Portoviejo, Ecuador; grew up in New York City, then Florida.
2009 and 2010: All-American at Georgia Tech; 2010 ACC Player of the Year.

people.name: Jaime E. Rodríguez O.
body: Jaime E. Rodríguez was born in Ecuador in 1940. UC Irvine says Quito, and a memorial in The Americas says Guayaquil. In 1948, when he was about eight, he and his mother, Beatriz Ordoñez, moved to the United States. He became a leading U.S. historian of Mexico and of Spanish America's independence era.

After a period in the U.S. Army, he earned a bachelor's degree in economics in 1965 and a master's in history in 1966, both from the University of Houston. In 1970 he received a Ph.D. in Mexican history from the University of Texas at Austin, where his adviser was the historian Nettie Lee Benson.

He taught Latin American history at California State University, Long Beach, from 1969 to 1973, then joined the University of California, Irvine, where he spent the rest of his career. He served as dean of graduate studies and research from 1980 to 1986 and directed the Mexico/Chicano Program from 1984 to 1992. He was a founding director of the campus's Latin American Studies Program, now the Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies. He also co-founded and edited the journal Mexican Studies/Estudios Mexicanos.

His books include The Forging of the Cosmic Race (1980), The Independence of Spanish America (1998) and "We Are Now the True Spaniards" (2012), a study of how Mexico became a federal republic. He died on June 27, 2022, after a long illness, at 82. His wife, the historian Linda Alexander Rodríguez, had died a month earlier.
keyFacts: 1940: Born in Ecuador; moved to the U.S. with his mother in 1948.
B.A. (1965) and M.A. (1966), University of Houston; Ph.D., University of Texas at Austin (1970).
1969–1973: Taught at California State University, Long Beach.
Joined UC Irvine in 1973; dean of graduate studies and research, 1980–1986.
Co-founded Mexican Studies/Estudios Mexicanos.
June 27, 2022: Died at age 82.

people.name: Lenín Moreno
body: Lenín Moreno was born on March 19, 1953, in Nuevo Rocafuerte, a small town in Ecuador's Amazon region. He became paraplegic in 1998 after being shot in the back during an attempted robbery in Quito, and he uses a wheelchair.

As Vice President of Ecuador from 2007 to 2013, he coordinated Misión Manuela Espejo, a door-to-door national disability study. Cuban and Venezuelan volunteers, working with Ecuadorian doctors, visited 221 cantons in all 24 provinces and identified 294,166 people with disabilities. The mission also gave out about 76,000 mobility aids and other equipment.

Deputies from his party proposed him for the Nobel Peace Prize, and Staffordshire University's guide gives the year as 2012. In December 2013 the United Nations Secretary-General appointed him Special Envoy on Disability and Accessibility, a post based in Geneva that he held for almost three years. He served as President of Ecuador from May 2017 to May 2021.

His public record is contested. On August 28, 2026, a panel of Ecuador's National Court in Quito convicted him of bribery in a case over the Coca Codo Sinclair hydroelectric plant and sentenced him to five years in prison and a ban from public office, Al Jazeera reports. He denies receiving any money and has said he will appeal, Gulf News reports. This page includes him for his disability work, and that work does not settle or excuse the case.
keyFacts: 1953: Born March 19 in Nuevo Rocafuerte, Ecuador.
1998: Became paraplegic after a shooting.
2007–2013: Vice President; Misión Manuela Espejo results presented December 2010.
December 2013: UN Special Envoy on Disability and Accessibility.
2017–2021: President of Ecuador.
August 28, 2026: Convicted of bribery; he denies it and has said he will appeal.

people.name: Xavier Torres Correa
body: In 1990, at 26, Xavier Torres Correa became quadriplegic while trying to protect his young nephews, the Australian journal Overland reported in 2013. He spent two years in Cuba, where he regained use of his hands. He returned to Ecuador in 1992 and joined the Association of Paraplegics of Pichincha, later becoming its president.

He went on to work with two national bodies: FENEDIF, the National Federation of Ecuadorians with a Physical Disability, and CONADIS, the national disability council. He told Overland that government support before 2007 was "very limited, almost non existent," and that disabled people in Ecuador had been "discriminated against by their own families." That is one person's view, not research. He also pointed to a law requiring companies with more than 25 employees to have disabled people as 4 percent of their staff.

As of October 2026, FENEDIF's site lists Xavier Torres as its president and a leader of the Pichincha association. It says he previously headed CONADIS and spent 2025 traveling the country to explain Ecuador's new Organic Law on Persons with Disabilities.

institutions.name: COPAL
aliases: Comunidades Organizando el Poder y la Acción Latina
COPAL (Comunidades Organizando el Poder y la Acción Latina)
institutions.location: Minneapolis (2712 E. Lake St.), with offices in Mankato (127 S. 2nd St. #100) and Rochester (1210½ 7th St. NW, Suite 216)
body: COPAL describes itself as a member-based organization, founded in 2018, that works to improve the quality of life of Latine families across Minnesota. It serves Latinos of every national origin. In July 2026 the Northeaster reported that most of its members are Ecuadorian, without giving a percentage. As of early 2024, COPAL's site reported more than 1,000 members.

From its Lake Street headquarters, COPAL runs a workers' center at the same address, the Centro de Trabajadores Primero de Mayo. Its other work includes MN Latino Vote, Know Your Rights resources and a community radio project, Radio Jornalera. In 2025 it launched the Immigrant Defense Network, which brings together more than 90 organizations. It is planning a Latino Center for Community Engagement at 2905 E. Lake St.

Sahan Journal reported in 2024 that asylum cases from Ecuador in Minnesota's immigration court had risen 900 percent over five years, and cited violence, economic distress and drought as reasons people left. A group of Ecuadorians called the TPS Collective backed a federal bill to give Ecuadorians Temporary Protected Status, which lets people from countries in crisis live and work legally in the U.S. for a time, and supported asylum seekers through COPAL. As of July 2026, the Northeaster reported, Ecuador had not been designated for that status.
keyFacts: 2018: Founded as a member-based Latino organization.
Programs include Centro de Trabajadores Primero de Mayo, MN Latino Vote, Radio Jornalera and Know Your Rights.
2025: Launched the Immigrant Defense Network, with more than 90 organizations.
Offices in Minneapolis, Mankato and Rochester.

institutions.name: Church of Saints Cyril and Methodius
aliases: Saints Cyril and Methodius Catholic Church
Ss Cyril and Methodius Catholic Church
body: According to the Archdiocese of Saint Paul and Minneapolis, the first Slovak Catholics settled in Minneapolis in 1875 and for many years worshiped with Polish Catholics at Holy Cross. They built their first church in 1893, moved to the present site in 1909 and finished the current brick church in 1917. The archdiocese says the parish has been mostly Hispanic since 1997, with many Spanish-speaking immigrants from Ecuador and other countries. As of October 2026 it lists several Spanish-language Masses each week.

In 2015 the Twin Cities Daily Planet, reprinting the Northeaster, reported that Ecuadorians were the largest group in the congregation. The parish hosts a celebration of Nuestra Señora de la Nube, Our Lady of the Cloud, which honors a believed appearance of Mary in the clouds in Ecuador. The New Year's Day observance in 2015 was the 15th held there. According to a church history quoted by the paper, Ecuadorians who had come from New York City prompted the celebration. In 2023 Fr. Fernando Ortega told The Catholic Spirit it had the largest Ecuadorian congregation in the area.
Sahan Journal reports that Northeast Minneapolis is informally called "Little Cuenca," after the Ecuadorian city.

institutions.name: El Colegio Charter School
body: El Colegio describes itself as a small public high school in Minneapolis that has served students in English and Spanish since 2000. It says its learning combines research-based teaching with the cultural and traditional practices of the families it serves.

In 2024 Sahan Journal reported that 44 of its 98 students were from Ecuador. Those are the numbers from one school year, and they may have changed. The school created a position to honor credits students had earned in Ecuador, since newly arrived students often started below their age-appropriate grade, and offered classes in Quichua, an Indigenous language spoken in Ecuador. On February 9, 2024, students celebrated Ecuadorian Carnaval.

2024: 44 of 98 students from Ecuador, by Sahan Journal's report.
Created a position to honor credits earned in Ecuador; offered Quichua classes.

institutions.name: Consejo Nacional para la Igualdad de Discapacidades (CONADIS), Ecuador
institutions.location: Av. 10 de Agosto N37-193, Quito, Ecuador
body: CONADIS is Ecuador's national disability equality council, based in Quito. It began as the Consejo Nacional de Discapacidades, created by Law 180, published on August 10, 1992. Ecuador's Ley Orgánica de Discapacidades was published on September 25, 2012, and last amended on May 6, 2019, according to Derecho Ecuador. FENEDIF, the national federation, reports a newer Organic Law on Persons with Disabilities that it was explaining around the country in 2025.

As of October 2026 its website offers disability statistics, online disability courses, regional technical offices, a list of health facilities with disability evaluation teams, and a directory of disability federations, associations and foundations. It is a home-country institution, not a Minnesota service.

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Ecuadorian families in Minnesota differ by region of origin, Indigenous or mestizo identity, language (Spanish, Kichwa, or both), faith, education and immigration history. We did not find a study of how Ecuadorian families in Minnesota or elsewhere in the United States understand disability, and research on Kichwa (also written Quichua) families is thinner still. What follows is a few small studies and abstracts from Ecuador, labeled as such, and general reporting on the community in Minnesota.
questions: Which language is most comfortable for you for this conversation: Spanish, Kichwa, English, or a mix? Is that the same for everyone in your family?
What do you and your family think about what's going on? What have others told you?
Who gave you a diagnosis or a label? Has it helped or got in the way?
What do you want a label or assessment to open up for you, and is there anything you want it to avoid?
Did you have services, records or a disability ID card in Ecuador? Would you like to use them here?
Who helps you make decisions, and who helps day to day? Would you like any of them here?
Are you already using healing or faith practices that matter to you? How can services fit around them?
What do your work hours, transportation and childcare allow? When and where would a meeting work?
Is there anything you want to know about who sees your information before we go further?
What words do you prefer for this, in Spanish, Kichwa or English?
Is there anything about how this began that you would like us to know? You don't have to say.

context.heading: What studies from Ecuador can and cannot tell you
body: A 2008 conference abstract on intellectual disability in Ecuador (Miranda-Galarza, Lancaster Disability Studies Conference) warns against treating Latin America as one culture. Drawing on fieldwork and family stories, it names six institutions that shape how the idea is talked about there: the church, the state, the media, NGOs, academia and the family. It argues that official diagnostic categories can reinforce negative stereotypes. The abstract does not describe specific beliefs.

A 2020 University of Sheffield doctoral thesis (Madrid Menéndez) spent three months with Kichwa people in Rukullacta, in Ecuador's Amazon. It found that local health practices reflect collective living, a relationship with nature, ancestors and spirits, enduring strength and knowledge gained through experience. The author warns that general descriptions of "Indigenous medicine" oversimplify and miss changes between generations. It is about one community and about health in general, not disability.

A 2019 undergraduate thesis at Universidad de las Américas (Fichamba Yamberla) set out to interview 8 Kichwa/Otavalo and 8 mestizo main caregivers of autistic children at a center in Otavalo. Its premise is that using only a medical model can leave families feeling unheard and lead them to stop treatment. The public abstract reports no findings, so we draw no conclusions from it.
We did not find any source showing beliefs such as disability as punishment, fate or a test from God among Ecuadorian families. Ask; do not assume.

context.heading: Family and caregiving: one small study
body: An undergraduate thesis at the Universidad de Cuenca (Campos Díaz and Narváez Coronel, 2016) used life stories from 5 of the 46 families with a disabled member served by the Sayausí health subcenter in Cuenca. Most described learning of the disability as a sad event that took a long time to adjust to. They spoke of uncertainty, fear of recurrence, cost, and discrimination from relatives, neighbors and society. Daily care usually fell to women close to the person. Families also described support from relatives as helping them. It is five families in one parish in Ecuador, and it describes no Minnesota family.

sources.label: Campos Díaz and Narváez Coronel, Universidad de Cuenca thesis (2016)

context.heading: Services in Ecuador before someone arrived
body: Ecuador's 2009–2010 Misión Manuela Espejo went door to door and identified 294,166 people with disabilities, about 2.43 percent of the population, according to IPS in December 2010. That count comes from one campaign and is not a total prevalence figure. IPS reported that volunteers found some people with severe disabilities living in extreme neglect. A critic in the same report said nongovernmental groups were left out.

So what a person experienced depends heavily on where and when. Some will have had a disability ID and services, and others may have had very little. Ask rather than guess. National law and disability bodies have also changed, and FENEDIF reports a newer law being explained around the country in 2025.

FENEDIF, Directiva

context.heading: Language access, including Kichwa
body: Kichwa Hatari, a New York collective, says Kichwa migrants are often overlooked among Ecuadorians and Latinos, and that interpreters are often unavailable in courts, schools and hospitals. Do not assume that a person from Ecuador speaks Spanish as a first language. If Kichwa is preferred, request a Kichwa interpreter and note any shortage in the record, rather than defaulting to a child or relative.

We did not find a documented source on Kichwa words for disability, or on Ecuadorian Spanish terms that carry stigma, so this page lists none. Ecuador's national council uses "personas con discapacidad". Use plain language, and short written summaries in Spanish, and read key points aloud for people who prefer spoken information.

context.heading: Immigration, work and time
body: Sahan Journal reported in November 2025, citing Syracuse University data, that 11,921 Ecuadorian cases were pending at the Fort Snelling Immigration Court. It also reported 1,920 pending Ecuadorian asylum cases in Minnesota as of 2024, the most of any group in the state. These count court cases, not people in the community, and they say nothing about any person's status or history. Many of those reported on hold work permits.

VisaVerge, a secondary news source, reported in November 2025 that local officials say families fear deportation even as they settle into schools and jobs, and that work authorization is slow. Before reading a missed appointment as cultural, check shifts, transport and fear of the office itself. Explain clearly what information goes to whom. Say that disability services are separate from immigration enforcement only if that is accurate for your program.

context.heading: Networks and strengths
body: VisaVerge reported in 2025 that Twin Cities Ecuadorians have held summer weekend volleyball games and picnics for nearly 30 years, and that newcomers often reach relatives or trusted contacts who help with housing and school enrollment. Sahan Journal has reported new Ecuadorian-owned markets, shops and food businesses along Central Avenue, in Columbia Heights and in south Minneapolis. We did not find a study of how these networks handle disability. Ask whether a person wants any of them involved.

We did not find an Ecuadorian-specific disability organization in Minnesota, or an Ecuadorian Deaf leader. Disabled Ecuadorians have organized their own associations at home, as FENEDIF's 57 affiliate associations show.

organizations.intro: Community life in Minnesota centers on Northeast Minneapolis and Columbia Heights, with newer markets in south Minneapolis. The Northeaster traces it to a handful of families from Cuenca in the late 1990s. An Archdiocese of Saint Paul and Minneapolis staff member estimated in 2023 that about 5 percent of Minnesota's roughly 350,000 Latino residents were from Ecuador; that is one estimate, not a count. We did not find a formal Ecuadorian association, sports league or festival committee in Minnesota, which does not mean none exists, and the consulate has organized community gatherings such as a meeting around a June 2026 World Cup match. Ecuadorian-owned businesses are also gathering places. Sahan Journal has reported on El Paraiso on Central Avenue, co-owned by Columbia Heights firefighter Bertha Orellana. The list below is a set of starting points for learning, and it is not complete. Being listed says nothing about who a person trusts.
